title: What to keep from Seneca
hook: time, friendship, reading, calm, and honesty about failure

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paulina, and the people who stayed beside Seneca to the end. Your line was beside him.

When you move house, there's a moment with every box: keep, or let go? Not everything from the old place fits in the new one. We're nearly done with Seneca: almost ninety days of letters and essays, and this week alone took us through gifts given and received, a grieving mother, a shameful letter from exile, a better letter to his own mother, and the long evening of his death. Before we move on, it's time to pack.
screen: `KEEP, OR LET GO?` → `NEARLY NINETY DAYS OF SENECA.` → `WHAT TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: Here are five candidates. You'll keep three. First, time, from the very first letter, which we'll reopen tomorrow: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." Everything else can be taken, Seneca says, and yet time is what we let leak away most carelessly. Second, friendship. Seneca's letters are one long friendship with Lucilius. He passes on an old line from the philosopher Hecato: if you want to be loved, love. This week added two more pictures of it: giving freely and forgetting, and receiving gladly, so the gift lands. Third, reading. Stay with a few good writers until they become part of you, he said early on, because a mind that's everywhere is nowhere. Fourth, calm. On Anger gave us the plainest cure: delay. Let the first rush pass, then judge. Fifth, honesty about failure. He told Lucilius he was not wise, only less bad each day. He admitted seasickness, tears, mistakes. And this week we saw a failure he didn't admit in the letter itself: flattery from exile. Maybe that's the strongest reason to keep this one. Seneca shows that a person can teach well, fall short of the teaching, and still be worth reading. There's no right answer. Some people keep time, because they're always behind. Some keep friendship, because they've been lonely. Some keep honesty about failure, because they're tired of pretending. Choose the three that would change an ordinary Tuesday.
screen: `TIME: NOTHING ELSE IS OURS.` · `FRIENDSHIP: TO BE LOVED, LOVE.` · `READING AND CALM.` · `HONESTY ABOUT FAILURE.` · then, large: `THREE KEEPERS.`

segments.voice: Picture five boxes labeled time, friendship, reading, calm and honesty about failure, and lift each one slowly, weighing how much it matters in your life right now. Choose three, and set the other two down gently; they'll wait. Hold your three for a while.
Tempus. Latin for time, the first keeper from Seneca's very first letter: one of five candidates, with friendship, reading, calm and honesty about failure, to choose three from. Today's word.
Your line: three keepers. The other two will wait on the shelf. That's day five hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca carry a few of his themes with them rather than his whole system: guarding time, tending friendships, reading deeply, delaying anger, and admitting their own failures.

chat.says: Is Seneca still worth reading, if he didn't live up to his own teaching?
options: Yes: he shows a person can teach well, fall short, and still be worth reading.
No: once a teacher fails his own teaching, nothing he wrote can be trusted.
Yes, because he never really fell short; the stories about him are rumors.
chat.meaning: Seneca admitted he wasn't wise, and his flattery from exile shows it. He still teaches well: falling short doesn't erase what's worth keeping.

Lucilius.meaning: Seneca's friend, to whom he wrote his letters
